metadata.summary: This European Glaucoma Society guide reviews evidence on newer glaucoma operations and devices and offers clinical guidance where evidence is limited. It addresses procedure selection, comparative efficacy and safety, and the management of complications. It also proposes standards for developing, evaluating and reporting studies of surgical innovations.

care_settings: cataract surgery combined with glaucoma surgery
target_population: patients with primary or secondary OAG
patients with coexistent glaucoma and cataract
surgeons and researchers evaluating glaucoma surgical innovations

conditions.name: glaucoma
conditions.description: A condition in which limiting progression and glaucoma-related visual disability guides treatment. Lowering intraocular pressure reduces the rate of progression, but the surgical target and choice of procedure depend on the individual patient.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual field deterioration may occur; its effect on vision-related quality-of-life measures may become detectable only in very advanced disease.

subtypes.name: open-angle glaucoma (OAG)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guide distinguishes primary and secondary OAG among the populations studied for surgical innovations.

subtypes.name: advanced glaucoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lower target intraocular pressure may be needed than procedures with modest pressure-lowering effects can provide.

subtypes.name: progressive disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Continuing progression affects surgical selection; trabecular implants are not intended for these patients.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Visualize the anterior chamber angle during trabecular surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During trabecular procedures; proficiency with this examination is required.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether the angle is open and assess its extent before selecting surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Angle closure is a contraindication to trabecular procedures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure intraocular pressure and enable comparisons across surgical trials.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline and follow-up in surgical trials.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Central corneal thickness can influence the measured value.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate visual function and visual field damage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In studies assessing functional outcomes; at least 2 preoperative visual field tests are required to establish a trial baseline.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Mean deviation or mean defect can describe function. Assessing progression accurately requires more frequent testing or longer follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess visual acuity, particularly as a surgical safety outcome.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before and after surgery in surgical studies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A reduction of >2 Snellen lines is generally considered clinically relevant and warrants reporting of its cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural measures such as RNFL/GCC thickness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Optional in surgical trials; imaging may be useful in long-term studies (>5 years).
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Short-term detection of structural change is limited, and advanced cases may show a floor effect in RNFL measurements.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide context for interpreting intraocular pressure measurements.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Optional as a descriptor in surgical studies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It may cause GAT readings to overestimate or underestimate intraocular pressure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess corneal endothelial safety after ocular surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline and follow-up in studies of surgical innovations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide calls for reporting the absolute count, percentage change and proportions of patients with losses exceeding 20, 30, and 40% from baseline.

staging.additional_rules: The guide uses mild, moderate and advanced disease when discussing surgical selection, but does not provide diagnostic definitions for these categories.

follow_up.schedule: For most safety and efficacy outcomes in surgical studies, recommended postoperative assessments occur at 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months; studies extending beyond 12 months may schedule visits every 6 months. Assessment at 1 day is recommended for techniques early in development. These are study-reporting time points, not a uniform schedule for routine care.
recommended_tests: Record visual field outcomes at appropriate study time points; progression assessments require more frequent testing or longer observation.
Assess BCVA as a safety outcome.
Monitor endothelial corneal cells (ECCs) as a surgical safety outcome.
Record postoperative complications and additional interventions.
long_term_effects: Long-term follow-up is important for identifying uncommon or delayed adverse effects of innovative glaucoma surgery.
Late endothelial cell loss was reported 48 months after CyPass® surgery and was a reason for the device's withdrawal.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: After a bleb-forming procedure, careful postoperative surveillance and management of the filtering bleb are necessary.

conditions.name: primary OAG
conditions.description: A primary open-angle glaucoma population included in the guide's assessment of innovative surgical procedures.

conditions.name: secondary OAG
conditions.description: A secondary open-angle glaucoma population included in the guide's assessment of innovative surgical procedures.

conditions.name: ocular hypertension (OHT)
conditions.description: A patient population included among studies considered in the guide's review of glaucoma surgical innovations.

conditions.name: advanced glaucoma
conditions.description: Advanced disease is considered separately in surgical selection because the need for substantial intraocular pressure reduction can make procedures with modest pressure-lowering effects unsuitable.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating visual function in advanced disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural outcomes when used in a surgical study.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A floor effect can limit RNFL measurements in advanced cases.

staging.additional_rules: The guide names advanced glaucoma but does not specify a threshold defining this stage.

conditions.name: coexistent glaucoma and cataract
conditions.description: Concurrent glaucoma and cataract creates a choice between staged surgery and cataract surgery combined with a glaucoma procedure. The guide bases this choice chiefly on glaucoma severity and preoperative intraocular pressure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform selection of a staged or combined surgical approach.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before surgery for coexistent glaucoma and cataract.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: High preoperative pressure favors consideration of a bleb-forming approach rather than MIGS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform selection of a staged or combined surgical approach.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before surgery for coexistent glaucoma and cataract.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide distinguishes mild, moderate and advanced disease for this decision.

staging.additional_rules: Glaucoma severity is considered as mild, moderate or advanced when selecting surgery, without formal definitions for these categories.

long_term_effects: Phacoemulsification performed later may impair the function of a bleb-forming device; the guide notes that this conclusion relies partly on extrapolation because direct data are limited.

therapies_index.name: Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Groups ab-interno glaucoma procedures that do not create a filtering bleb, including trabecular and suprachoroidal approaches.
key_toxicities: Complications can occur despite a safety profile generally considered better than that of bleb-forming procedures.

therapies_index.name: iStent®
therapies_index.mechanism: Bypasses the trabecular meshwork to direct aqueous humour into Schlemm’s canal.
approved_indications: Approved in 2012 for mild-to-moderate open-angle glaucoma (OAG) when combined with cataract surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Inserted ab-interno into Schlemm’s canal; it is used mainly alongside cataract surgery, although standalone use may be considered in special circumstances.

therapies_index.name: iStent inject®
therapies_index.mechanism: A trabecular stent intended to bypass the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm’s canal.
therapies_index.administration: An injector can deliver up to two devices into Schlemm’s canal.

therapies_index.name: iStent W®
therapies_index.mechanism: A trabecular stent intended to bypass the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm’s canal.
therapies_index.administration: An injector can deliver up to two devices into Schlemm’s canal.

therapies_index.name: Hydrus®
therapies_index.mechanism: Bypasses the trabecular meshwork and expands Schlemm’s canal over 3 clock hours, potentially reaching multiple collector channels.
therapies_index.administration: Inserted into Schlemm’s canal through a clear corneal incision after pre-incision of the trabecular meshwork; it is used mainly with cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: ABiC™
therapies_index.mechanism: Dilates Schlemm’s canal through catheterization and viscoelastic injection.
therapies_index.administration: After trabecular meshwork pre-incision, an illuminated catheter cannulates Schlemm’s canal over 360°; high molecular weight viscoelastic is injected every two clock hours as the catheter is withdrawn.

therapies_index.name: OMNI® Surgical System
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides a Schlemm’s canal procedure similar to ABiC™.

therapies_index.name: Trabectome®
therapies_index.mechanism: Disrupts the trabecular meshwork so aqueous humour can reach Schlemm’s canal directly.
therapies_index.administration: Trabeculotomy is performed under intraoperative gonioscopy with an electrocautery handpiece that also irrigates and aspirates; 60°–120° of the nasal angle is treated.

therapies_index.name: Kahook Dual Blade®
therapies_index.mechanism: Cuts the trabecular meshwork during nonthermal trabeculotomy.
therapies_index.administration: Used as a cutting instrument for trabeculotomy.

therapies_index.name: GATT
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a circumferential trabeculotomy to permit aqueous humour to reach Schlemm’s canal.
therapies_index.administration: An illuminated microcatheter is advanced through Schlemm’s canal for 360° and then pulled through the trabecular meshwork.

therapies_index.name: Prolene GATT
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses a technique similar to GATT to create a trabeculotomy.
therapies_index.administration: Does not require the specific catheter described for GATT.

therapies_index.name: CyPass®
therapies_index.mechanism: Connects the anterior chamber to the suprachoroidal space to improve uveoscleral outflow.
therapies_index.administration: A 6.35 mm implant placed in the supraciliary space by an ab-interno approach; voluntarily withdrawn from the market in August 2018.
key_toxicities: Late endothelial cell loss was identified 48 months after surgery and might have been related to implant position.

Studies of its addition to cataract surgery reported increased loss of more than 2 lines of vision at medium- and long-term follow-up; endothelial cell density reduction >30% occurred in 27.2% of participants.

therapies_index.name: MiniJect®
therapies_index.mechanism: A supraciliary implant intended to improve uveoscleral outflow.
therapies_index.administration: Placed in the supraciliary space using an ab-interno approach.

therapies_index.name: Xen 45®
therapies_index.mechanism: Diverts aqueous humour from the anterior chamber to the subconjunctival space through a gel stent.
approved_indications: The Xen® gel stent is approved for ab-interno implantation through a clear corneal incision.
therapies_index.administration: For the Xen® gel stent, MMC is recommended as a subconjunctival injection before surgery, commonly at 10-40 μg. An off-label ab externo approach has been described for unusual circumstances.
key_toxicities: In a comparison with trabeculectomy, the gel stent arm had surgical complications in 2 (2.1%) eyes and clinical hypotony in 1.1%; 23.2% underwent needling.
Potentially serious complications of bleb-forming procedures include hypotony, bleb-related infection and device exposure.
monitoring: Careful postoperative bleb assessment and management are required.

therapies_index.name: PreserFlo®
therapies_index.mechanism: Drains aqueous humour from the anterior chamber to the subconjunctival or sub-Tenon’s space.
therapies_index.administration: Implanted ab externo through a scleral mini tunnel after creating a fornix-based conjunctival bleb and applying MMC.
key_toxicities: In a comparison with trabeculectomy, vision-threatening complications occurred in 1.0% of the PreserFlo® microshunt group, and hypotony requiring intervention occurred in 2.0% (8/395).
Potentially serious complications of bleb-forming procedures include hypotony, bleb-related infection and device exposure.
monitoring: Careful postoperative bleb assessment and management are required.

therapies_index.name: trabeculectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a filtering pathway for aqueous humour.
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes augmentation with antimetabolites and postoperative bleb management.
key_toxicities: In the cited comparison with PreserFlo®, vision-threatening complications occurred in 0.8% of the trabeculectomy group and hypotony requiring intervention in 7.6% (10/131).
In the cited comparison with Xen 45®, clinical hypotony occurred in 22.7% of the trabeculectomy arm.

therapies_index.name: phacoemulsification
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes a cataract.
approved_indications: Cataract in a patient who also has glaucoma.
therapies_index.administration: When staged surgery is appropriate, phacoemulsification is considered first; in combined procedures, it is performed before device insertion.

therapies_index.name: Hydrus® combined with phacoemulsification
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines cataract removal with trabecular bypass and expansion of Schlemm’s canal.
therapies_index.administration: Phacoemulsification precedes device insertion in a combined procedure.

therapies_index.name: iStent® combined with phacoemulsification
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines cataract removal with trabecular bypass into Schlemm’s canal.
approved_indications: Mild-to-moderate open-angle glaucoma (OAG) in conjunction with cataract surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Phacoemulsification precedes device insertion in a combined procedure.

therapies_index.name: Mitomycin C
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits scarring in filtering surgery, contributing to lower IOP.
therapies_index.administration: Used off-label in filtering surgery. For Xen® gel stent implantation, it is injected beneath the conjunctiva before surgery at a commonly used dose of 10-40 μg; it is also applied during PreserFlo® implantation.

therapies_index.name: 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)
therapies_index.mechanism: Used as an antimetabolite to inhibit scarring in filtering surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Used off-label in filtering surgery; antifibrotic agents may also be used with bleb needling or revision.

therapies_index.name: topical steroids
therapies_index.administration: After bleb-forming device surgery, postoperative steroid treatment is recommended using a strategy similar to that for trabeculectomy.

therapies_index.name: antibiotics
therapies_index.administration: Recommended postoperatively after bleb-forming device surgery, with a regimen similar to that used after trabeculectomy.

therapies_index.name: IOP-lowering drops
therapies_index.mechanism: Lower intraocular pressure.
therapies_index.administration: Given topically; criteria for restarting or escalating treatment after surgery should be defined in a trial protocol.
monitoring: Record the number of topical active principles and the number and percentage of patients receiving medication at each study time point.

therapies_index.name: bleb needling
therapies_index.administration: Antifibrotic agents are recommended in conjunction with needling. The guide advises against repeated needlings.
monitoring: Record the number of postoperative interventions required.

therapies_index.name: bleb revision
therapies_index.administration: Surgical, particularly open, revision is preferred over repeated needling; antifibrotic agents are recommended with revision.
monitoring: Record the number of postoperative interventions required.

therapies_index.name: suture lysis
therapies_index.administration: Described as a postoperative intervention for IOP control.
monitoring: Report its use even though it is not classified as a surgical failure event.

therapies_index.name: Nd:YAG laser goniopuncture
monitoring: Report its use even though it is not classified as a surgical failure event.

therapies_index.name: antimetabolite injections
monitoring: Report their use even though they are not classified as surgical failure events.

toxicities.incidence: Endothelial cell density reduction >30% was reported in 27.2% of participants in the safety evidence cited for Cypass®.
recognition: Endothelial cell loss was identified 48 months after surgery; implant position was considered a possible contributor.
prevention: CyPass® was voluntarily withdrawn from the market in August 2018 because of long-term safety concerns.

toxicities.incidence: In the cited Cypass® comparison with cataract surgery alone, loss of more than 2 lines of vision occurred in 11 per 1000 versus 0 per 1000 at medium-term follow-up and 112 per 1000 versus 60 per 1000 at long-term follow-up. For Hydrus® combined with cataract surgery versus cataract surgery alone, the RR for loss of two or more lines at long-term follow-up was 0.5 (95% CI 0.1 to 1.5); the evidence did not establish a definite safety difference.
recognition: Measure best-corrected visual acuity before and after surgery using standardized methods and report the causes of vision loss.
toxicities.grading: The guide describes loss of ≥ 3 lines on an ETDRS as moderate visual loss and loss of ≥ 6 lines as severe visual loss. Table 7 separately defines Mild BCVA Loss, Moderate BCVA Loss, Severe BCVA Loss and Blinding BCVA Loss.

recognition: Permanent loss of 5-10 ETDRS letters or an equivalent amount of vision.
Permanent loss of 10–20 ETDRS letters or an equivalent amount of vision.
Permanent loss of 20 or more ETDRS letters or an equivalent amount of vision, without loss of light perception.
Permanent loss of vision to no light perception (NLP).

toxicities.incidence: In the PreserFlo® microshunt versus trabeculectomy comparison, hypotony requiring intervention occurred in 2.0% (8/395) versus 7.6% (10/131), respectively. In the Xen 45® gel stent versus trabeculectomy comparison, clinical hypotony occurred in 1.1% versus 22.7%, respectively.
recognition: IOP <6 mmHg accompanied by choroidal detachment, hypotony maculopathy or reduced anterior chamber depth, or IOP < 6 mmHg requiring surgery to reverse a hypotony-related complication.
prevention: Patients considering bleb-forming surgery should be informed of the possibility of serious complications, including hypotony.

recognition: IOP <6 mmHg without an accompanying complication. The guide distinguishes low IOP measurements from clinically relevant, symptomatic hypotony.
Dome-shaped elevation extending posteriorly from the peripheral retina on fundus examination or imaging; this category includes serous choroidal effusion and blood-filled suprachoroidal haemorrhage.
The iris–cornea distance is less than before surgery. Grade 0 has no iris–cornea contact; Grade 1 has peripheral iris–cornea contact.
The iris–cornea distance is less than before surgery. Grade 2 involves complete iris–cornea contact without lens–cornea contact; Grade 3 involves lens–cornea apposition.
A positive Seidel test at any site, including the edge of a filtering bleb.
Blood visible in the anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination; Grade 0 denotes circulating RBC in the AC.

toxicities.incidence: For Hydrus® combined with cataract surgery versus cataract surgery alone, the RR of postoperative hyphema was 1.0 (95% CI 0.1 to 11.1); the evidence did not establish a definite safety difference.
recognition: Blood is visible in the anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination. Grade 1 denotes a visible blood level that does not fill the AC; Grade 2 denotes blood filling the AC.

toxicities.incidence: For Hydrus® combined with cataract surgery versus cataract surgery alone, the RR of an IOP spike over 10 mmHg was 0.4 (95% CI 0.1 to 1.2), without a definite safety difference. For iStent® combined with cataract surgery versus cataract surgery alone, the RR of an IOP spike exceeding 10 mmHg was 0.2 (95% CI 0.1 to 0.7); that estimate was based on just one participant in each group.
recognition: Table 7 defines this event as an IOP increase of 10 mmHg relative to preoperative IOP.
Lens opacity accompanied by loss of 10 ETDRS letters or an equivalent amount from baseline, or lens opacity necessitating surgery.
Corneal oedema lasting over 4 weeks after surgery despite topical treatment.
Anterior chamber cells at SUN grade > 1+ cell that remain unresolved after 6 weeks postoperatively.
Purulent involvement of both aqueous and vitreous, with cells present in the AC and vitreous.
A white bleb containing mucopurulent material with marked surrounding conjunctival injection; AC inflammation may occur, but vitreous inflammation is absent.
prevention: Counsel patients that bleb-forming procedures can cause serious bleb-related infection.

recognition: Tissue no longer covers some part of a glaucoma implant, leaving that part directly in contact with the ocular surface.
prevention: Counsel patients that device exposure can be a serious complication of bleb-forming procedures.

recognition: Separation of any extent between the ciliary body and scleral spur, identified by gonioscopy or imaging.
Drooping of the upper eyelid that affects the visual field or prompts surgical correction.
Clinically apparent blockage of an implanted drainage device or a sclerostomy, regardless of where or how the blockage occurs.
A shallower central AC caused by forward displacement of the irido-lenticular diaphragm, with normal or elevated IOP, without choroidal detachment or pupillary block.
Intraretinal fluid of any amount in the macula, detectable by fundus examination or imaging.
Separation of neurosensory retina from retinal pigment epithelium on fundus examination or imaging.
An implant, or part of it, occupies an unintended position without having migrated from a previously correct position.
Blood within the vitreous cavity identified clinically or by imaging.
Binocular double vision attributable to ocular misalignment in any gaze position.
A sharply demarcated depression with intact epithelium over dehydrated, thinned corneal stroma.
A postoperative corneal epithelial defect apparent on slit-lamp examination.
Abnormal attachments between peripheral iris and the irido-corneal angle.
Patient-reported ocular pain, discomfort, burning, foreign-body sensation or tearing that arises or persists after 6 weeks from surgery.
Retinal haemorrhages after an abrupt decrease in IOP.
Postoperative movement of an implant, or part of it, away from its original intended position.

recommended_regimens.name: Hydrus® combined with phacoemulsification

artifacts.title: Table 6. IDEAL phases

rows: Results in a case report or a short case series describing the first use of a new technique in humans, often spurred by the need of a novel solution to a clinical situation. The Declaration of Helsinki highlights the significance of transparent reporting of research procedures and encourages prospective registration.44 Despite the apparent simplicity of applying these principles, the early stages of innovation may only become obvious in hindsight. A surgeon may first use a novel method to solve an otherwise difficult situation. Upon repetition, the surgeon may become conscious of having uncovered something possibly beneficial. Consequently, the first two steps of this model may be substantially finished before the novel character of the procedure is recognized. Transparency is required in patient selection, the informed consent procedure, and the description of the setting (including operator/team characteristics), location, and timing. In addition, a clear and comprehensive explanation of the technique/device, including patient safety monitoring procedures and appropriate pre- and post procedure care, must be included. Visual aids like pictures and videos are advantageous, and each patient’s adverse consequences must be documented. The outcome measures used should be standardised and validated. Based on the findings of Phase 1, it will be possible to determine whether it is desirable to continue with further patients and to address potential risks and preventive measures.45

Will lead to case series reporting the results after refinement of the technique. Reporting during this phase must include the following: selection criteria, eligible patients selected, a clear description of the procedure detailing the variation and clinically relevant outcomes and complications. Whenever feasible, all relevant result data should be integrated into a complete table or graph so that the link between method adjustments and outcomes may be readily shown. Learning curves are also a significant factor in this phase, and clear sequential outcome reporting of all cases should be conducted with no omissions. Phase 2a results will be used to evaluate whether the technique and outcomes have reached stability in the hands of the current team and to establish whether the technique is ready for evaluation in a prospective, multicentre IDEAL phase 2b study. The surgeon, the institution, and their ethical committee should reach a consensus on who is accountable for ensuring risk minimization.45

Entails the exploration of the new technique using prospective and collaborative cohort studies. At this stage an assessment metric for how well the operator or team adheres to the methodology might be beneficial. Furthermore, documenting the operator’s or team’s learning curve using recognised objective quality indicators may be advantageous. Detailed descriptions of the primary and secondary outcome measures and statistical methodologies are needed. It is critical to consider how to develop and execute future RCT studies while considering surgeon preferences. Concerning the scheduling of randomised trials, theoretical justifications for early randomisation are weighed against practical considerations for delay. The learning curve will probably influence which surgeons engage in randomised trials and when they do so. Phase 2b will provide the interpretation of data and evaluation of the suitability of proceeding to an RCT or a pilot/feasibility study. In this regard, consensus should have been obtained on the following:
– Standard technique (including accepted variants) and quality standards based on experience
– Target patient population and indications
– Outcome measure(s) (including estimated power calculation of the primary outcome)
– Comparator treatment for a trial
– Willingness among operators and patients to accept randomization.45

In the previous stages, the focus was on making a new technique and describing its results. In stage 3, the goal is to determine how well this new technique works compared with current standards. The most important thing is to determine the best comparator. At this stage, randomised controlled trials are the gold standard for comparing efficacy between conventional and innovative interventions. Surgical randomised studies may be impractical for ethical or logistical reasons, such as recruiting challenges or lack of equipoise among surgeons. In these instances, other designs may be needed, such as parallel group non-randomised studies, expertise-based randomised trials, tracker trials, controlled interrupted-time series studies and step-wedge designs.36,46-48

Focuses on long-term evaluation, ideally through prospective databases and registries to assess innovations for rare side effects, long-term outcomes and for variations in outcome. Only key outcomes should be pursued to encourage complete data entry.

rows: Bar Chart Unique harms are arranged along x-axis in an order of the authors’ choice (e.g., descending or ascending effect size, alphabetical).

Dot Plot Unique harms are arranged along the y-axis in an order of the authors’ choice.

• Incidence/occurrence of each harm by trial arm (x-axis on the left panel of the figure)

• Expandable format using a panel approach
• High value for communicating harms as rated by experts
• Figure becomes long with many events (each unique harm gets a row)
Heatmap Unique harms are arranged along the y-axis in an order of the authors’ choice.

• Subgroups of participants experiencing each harm (x-axis)

• Moderate value for communicating harms as rated by experts

• Difficult to understand
• Figure becomes long with many events (each unique harm gets a row)
• Overwhelming with too many events and subgroups
Volcano Plot Unique harms are represented by bubbles placed on an X-Y grid.

• Overall occurrence of each harm (size of bubble)
• P value (y-axis and opacity of bubble)
• Trial arm positively associated with each harm (colour)

• P value (colour of each harm’s points)
• Duration between each event (length of each vector)
