document_sections.heading: Prologue
document_sections.content: Trabeculectomy with antimetabolites has long been the mainstay of glaucoma surgery, complemented by drainage tubes. Newer procedures, particularly MIGS, seek to improve safety, but their comparative efficacy and place alongside conventional surgery require evaluation. This guide examines the evidence for surgical innovations, offers clinical guidance where evidence is insufficient, and proposes standards for future studies. Treatment decisions must remain individualized: no single operation is appropriate for every patient. The EGS emphasizes that successful implementation of innovation depends on high-quality evidence.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Glaucoma surgery now offers substantially more options than trabeculectomy and drainage devices. Some new techniques entered practice before adequate evidence was available, and others were abandoned. Inconsistent surgical trial methods and outcomes hinder interpretation and comparison. The guide therefore aims to review evidence on novel devices, advise on procedures already used despite insufficient evidence, and harmonize trial design and reporting. Its clinical guidance addresses questions identified through a European survey and expert consensus, concentrating on procedures with enough collective experience to discuss. Core outcome reporting, a sample CRF, and guidance on study designs and complications are intended to improve future evidence. The group could not recommend some emerging technologies because its experience was insufficient.

document_sections.heading: 2. Definitions and surgical technical overview
document_sections.content: The guide distinguishes MIGS, defined in the 5th Ed. EGS Guidelines as ab-interno procedures that do not create a bleb, from subconjunctival bleb-forming surgery performed ab-interno or ab externo. Diagram 1 identifies the included procedures. The chapter covers techniques for which sufficient evidence was available when it was written.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS)
document_sections.content: Authors have described MIGS as potentially offering favorable safety, rapid recovery, and ease of use. In theory, tissue-sparing operations could permit earlier, more individualized intervention based on age, disease stage, progression, anatomy, and comorbidity, including an aim to reduce treatment burden or improve comfort and vision-related quality of life. Their pressure-lowering effect is nevertheless less than that of filtration surgery. The guide divides MIGS into trabecular procedures or devices and suprachoroidal devices.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.1 Trabecular procedures and devices
document_sections.content: Procedures directed through the trabecular meshwork toward Schlemm’s canal include stenting and tissue-disrupting approaches. They require intraoperative gonioscopy and repositioning of the patient and microscope. Contraindications include angle closure, prior trauma, visible congenital angle anomalies, and increased episcleral venous pressure.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.1.1 Stenting procedures:
document_sections.content: Stents bypass the trabecular meshwork to direct aqueous humour into Schlemm’s canal. iStent® was approved in 2012 for mild-to-moderate open-angle glaucoma alongside cataract surgery. Its original form was a heparin-coated, nonferromagnetic, L-shaped titanium implant; iStent inject® and iStent W® are smaller conical versions delivered by an injector capable of placing up to two devices. Hydrus® is a curved, open nitinol scaffold introduced through a clear corneal incision after trabecular pre-incision. It expands Schlemm’s canal across 3 clock hours with the intention of reaching several collector channels.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.1.2 Dilating procedures:
document_sections.content: For ABiC™, a light-tipped catheter enters Schlemm’s canal after trabecular pre-incision, traverses 360°, and is withdrawn while high-molecular-weight viscoelastic is injected every two clock hours. OMNI® Surgical System offers a similar approach.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.1.3 Disrupting procedures
document_sections.content: These ab-interno techniques remove or divide trabecular meshwork so aqueous humour can enter Schlemm’s canal directly. Trabectome® uses an electrocautery, irrigation, and aspiration handpiece under gonioscopy to treat 60°–120° of the nasal angle. Kahook Dual Blade® (KDB) performs trabeculotomy using a nonthermal cutting instrument. In GATT, an illuminated catheter passes around the canal for 360° and is pulled through the meshwork to form a circumferential trabeculotomy. A version without a dedicated catheter is termed Prolene GATT.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.2 Suprachoroidal devices
document_sections.content: Suprachoroidal implants seek to create controlled cyclodialysis, connecting the anterior chamber with the suprachoroidal space to increase uveoscleral outflow. CyPass® is a 6.35 mm polyamide ab-interno implant. Its manufacturer withdrew it in August 2018 because of late endothelial cell loss at 48 months, possibly associated with implant position. MiniJect® and other ab-interno supraciliary implants were in clinical use, but evidence remained sparse and trials were ongoing.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Bleb-forming devices
document_sections.content: Subconjunctival devices establish an aqueous outflow route to the subconjunctival space. Tube length and internal diameter influence flow under Poiseuille’s law; theoretically, this can limit postoperative hypotony while substantially lowering IOP. A clinician experienced in bleb management should oversee postoperative care. Conjunctival manipulation and cytotoxic agents mean these operations should not be described as minimally invasive. Off-label 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or Mitomycin C (MMC) is used to inhibit scarring; systematic reviews have shown associated IOP reduction. Xen® gel stent is a porcine-gelatine tube with 45 and 63 µm lumen options. Subconjunctival MMC before implantation is recommended; the commonly used dose is 10-40 μg. Its approved route is ab-interno through a clear corneal incision, while an ab externo approach has been described off-label for unusual situations. PreserFlo®, formerly InnFocus microshunt, is implanted ab externo through a small scleral tunnel after conjunctival bleb preparation and MMC application.

document_sections.heading: 3. Literature review and recommendations
document_sections.content: The guide reviews evidence and consensus concerning the effectiveness, efficacy, and safety of the techniques described in Chapter 2, alongside identified knowledge gaps. New operations warrant assessment of both short- and long-term outcomes before widespread adoption.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1 Identification of key clinical questions
document_sections.content: Key questions were identified through convenience sampling of EGS members with attention to geographical representation.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.2 Summarizing available evidence
document_sections.content: The review sought RCTs and systematic reviews of surgical innovations involving trabecular bypass, trabecular stenting or disruption, suprachoroidal implants, and subconjunctival bleb-forming devices. Eligible participants had primary or secondary OAG or OHT; procedures could be combined with cataract surgery or performed alone. Comparators included cataract extraction, other innovative operations, trabeculectomy, laser trabeculoplasty, and medication. Most included publications used the proportion not taking IOP-lowering drops as their primary outcome, although EGS Guidelines do not endorse that outcome. Secondary outcomes included IOP and drop-count changes, further glaucoma procedures, complications, and HRQoL. When available, outcomes were evaluated at short-term (<6 months), medium-term (6 to 18 months), long-term (>18 to 36 months), and beyond 36 months.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.3 Study selection
document_sections.content: The authors used an overview and network meta-analysis of six Cochrane reviews published between December 2018 and February 2021. They also identified Fourteen non-Cochrane reviews; Six met their methodological acceptability criteria and were added. A review was considered reliable only if it specified study eligibility, searched comprehensively, assessed study bias, used appropriate meta-analysis methods where relevant, and aligned its conclusions with its findings. Failure on one or more criteria made a review unreliable.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.4 Data synthesis
document_sections.content: The authors summarized systematic-review estimates and described comparisons by procedure. Where Cochrane data were pooled, they reported estimates with confidence intervals and heterogeneity; otherwise, they used trial estimates. Random-effects NMAs examined outcomes available through two or more comparisons at the longest follow-up: medication-free status, unmedicated IOP change, and change in drop count. The analyses assumed a common outcome-specific network heterogeneity parameter and an equal phacoemulsification effect across MIGS combinations; estimates were presented with 95% confidence and prediction intervals. Two investigators independently extracted and validated additional RCT data. The large PreserFlo®-versus-trabeculectomy RCT was judged at high risk of bias because investigators were unmasked and many post hoc analyses were reported. Following synthesis, the EGS Surgery Task Force met face-to-face twice in 2021 to address surveyed questions. It did not recommend procedures for which most members lacked expertise. Under GRADE methodology, evidence was categorized ‘high’, ‘moderate’, ‘low’, or ‘very low’; recommendations were ‘strong’ when benefits clearly outweighed risks and ‘weak’ when that balance remained unclear and use was optional. Experts also agreed to compile a choosing-wisely list.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1 Trabecular stenting devices
document_sections.content: The evidence analysis covers iStent® and Hydrus®. In direct RCT comparisons with cataract extraction alone, adding Hydrus® or iStent® increased medication-free status at medium-term follow-up: respectively RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.8, and RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.6, each based on 2 trials. Certainty was moderate for Hydrus® and very low for iStent®. The Hydrus® effect persisted at 2 years (RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.9); comparable long-term results for other techniques were unavailable. In 1 stand-alone-device RCT, Hydrus® exceeded iStent® for medium-term medication-free status (RR 1.9, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.1; low certainty). An additional stand-alone iStent® did not improve the medication-free proportion. NMA favored Hydrus® over iStent® for this outcome (RR for iStent® versus Hydrus® 0.8, 95% CI 0.6 to 0.9, 95% PI 0.6 to 1.1). Compared with cataract extraction alone, adding Hydrus® lowered long-term IOP by an additional 2.0 mmHg (95% CI -2.7 to -1.3 mmHg; two trials; moderate certainty). Adding iStent® produced an additional short-term reduction of 5.0 mmHg (95% CI -7.5 to -2.5 mmHg; 3 trials; very low certainty), but the medium-term difference was not statistically significant. In 1 stand-alone RCT, Hydrus® lowered IOP 3.1 mmHg more than iStent® (95% CI 2.0 to 4.2 mmHg; moderate evidence); NMA suggested a smaller statistically significant effect of 1.9 mmHg (95% CI 0.3 to 3.6, 95% PI to -1.9 to 5.8). Neither two iStent® nor one stand-alone iStent® lowered medium-term IOP more than medication. Two or three iStent® improved medium-term IOP lowering relative to one, without a short- or long-term difference. Evidence about daily drop counts was low or very low and not consistently available. Against cataract extraction alone, Hydrus® plus extraction reduced long-term daily drops by 0.41 (95% CI -0.6 to -0.3; 2 trials); iStent® plus extraction reduced medium-term daily drops by 0.42 (range -0.6 to -0.2; 3 trials). Stand-alone Hydrus® reduced medium-term use by 0.6 more drops than iStent® (95% CI -1.0 to -0.2; 1 trial); NMA estimated 0.2 drops (95% CI -0.1 to 0.6, 95% PI -0.5 to 0.9). Loss of two or more vision lines was the most prevalent severe complication reported. Weak evidence did not establish a definite safety difference between Hydrus® plus cataract surgery and cataract surgery alone: long-term RR for loss of two or more lines was 0.5 (95% CI 0.1 to 1.5), RR for an IOP increase over 10 mmHg was 0.4 (95% CI 0.1 to 1.2), and RR for postoperative hyphema was 1.0 (95% CI 0.1 to 11.1). Combined iStent® surgery showed fewer IOP increases exceeding 10 mmHg than cataract surgery alone (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.7), but the estimate rested on just one participant in each group. A cited 5-year Hydrus®-phacoemulsification study reported 29.5% vs 33.8% of eyes at IOP 18 mmHg or less without medication, 66% vs 46% medication-free, and subsequent glaucoma surgery in 2.4% vs 6.2%, compared with phacoemulsification alone; its post hoc visual-field progression rates were –0.26 dB/y vs –0.49 dB/y. The guide concludes that Hydrus® with phacoemulsification is probably more effective than one iStent® with phacoemulsification for IOP and medication reduction, while evidence for stand-alone use is low.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation
document_sections.content: Hydrus® and iStent® can reduce medication use, but their long-term IOP effect is comparatively modest. They are generally paired with phacoemulsification when cataract surgery is needed. They are not recommended for advanced glaucoma with uncontrolled IOP or progressive disease. Available surgical safety findings are favorable, although more long-term evidence is needed. Table 1 summarizes expected medication reduction, usual combined use, potential stand-alone use under special circumstances, and the limits of long-term knowledge; it also notes that lowering drop burden rather than IOP is not the traditional glaucoma-surgery objective described in the EGS Guidelines 5th Ed.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2 Trabecular procedures
document_sections.content: Evidence is limited for Trabectome®, Kahook Dual Blade® (KDB), GATT, and ABiC™. At medium-term follow-up, a direct comparison found that Trabectome with cataract extraction did not produce a greater medication-free proportion than trabeculectomy with cataract extraction.

document_sections.heading: Consensus Notes
document_sections.content: Participants had insufficient experience with these trabecular techniques to establish practice-guiding consensus.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Interpretation
document_sections.content: The panel considered the published evidence too sparse to support clinical recommendations on these techniques; their effectiveness and safety remain substantially uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3 Suprachoroidal devices
document_sections.content: Although Cypass® left the market in 2018, a direct trial found that adding it to cataract surgery increased medium-term medication-free status (RR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.5; 1 trial; moderate certainty). An indirect NMA suggested a similar likelihood to iStent® (RR 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.3, 95% PI 0.7 to 1.4). The addition lowered medium-term IOP by another 2.3 mmHg (95% CI -3.0 to -1.6 mmHg; 1 trial; high certainty); NMA suggested IOP effects similar to Hydrus®. One report found drop-count changes of -1.2 with Cypass® plus cataract extraction versus -0.7 with extraction alone. High-certainty evidence associated Cypass® addition with more loss of over 2 vision lines at medium-term (11 per 1000 versus 0 per 1000) and long-term follow-up (112 per 1000 versus 60 per 1000); relative effects were not analyzed. COMPASS XT and NCT03273907 supplied high-certainty evidence of increased loss of two or more lines at these follow-ups, with endothelial cell density falling >30% in 27.2% of participants.

document_sections.heading: Consensus Notes
document_sections.content: The panel observed moderate IOP reduction with Cypass® alone and when combined with phacoemulsification.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Recommendation
document_sections.content: Cypass® was withdrawn because of long-term safety concerns. Other devices remained at an early development stage.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4 Bleb-forming devices
document_sections.content: The analysis concerns PreserFlo® microshunt and Xen 45® gel stent. In separate RCT comparisons against trabeculectomy, medication-free proportions at 1 year were 71.6% vs. 84.8% for PreserFlo® and trabeculectomy, and 61.2% vs 70.5% for Xen 45® and trabeculectomy, respectively; neither trial’s authors reported whether its difference was statistically significant. In the PreserFlo® arm, mean IOP ± SD changed from 21.1±4.9 mmHg to 14.3±4.3 mmHg at year 1 (−29.1%; P<0.01); the trabeculectomy arm changed from 21.1±5.0 mmHg to 11.1±4.3 mmHg (−45.4%; P<0.01). One-year success was 53.9% versus 72.7%, respectively (P<0.01). In the other RCT, Xen 45® IOP fell from 23.1±5.8 mmHg to 14.4±4.1 (P<0.001), versus 22.6±5.7mmHg to 11.8±3.5mmHg after trabeculectomy (P<0.001). At one year, complete and qualified success were 44.2% and 62.1% with Xen 45®, versus 59.1% and 72.7% with trabeculectomy; treatment differences were not statistically significant (p≥0.144 for both success rates). The RCTs did not share a success definition. At one year, PreserFlo® patients used a mean 0.6±1.1 glaucoma medications versus baseline 3.1±1.0 (P<0.01); trabeculectomy patients used 0.3±0.9 versus baseline 3.0±0.9 (P<0.01). In the Xen comparison, topical medication counts changed from 2.8 to 0.6 at 12 months for Xen and from 2.5 to 0.3 for trabeculectomy; both within-arm reductions were statistically significant. Vision-threatening complications occurred in 1.0% with PreserFlo® versus 0.8% with trabeculectomy. Hypotony requiring treatment affected 2.0% (8/395) versus 7.6% (10/131), respectively. In the Xen trial, surgical complications involved 2 (2.1%) eyes versus 3 (6.8%) trabeculectomy eyes; clinical hypotony occurred in 1.1% versus 22.7%, respectively. Needling was performed in 23.2% of Xen 45 eyes versus 18.2% of trabeculectomy eyes. Excluding laser suture lysis, postoperative intervention was required in 34.7% versus 40.9% (P=0.024).

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5 Results from comparison studies and Consensus notes
document_sections.content: High-quality studies of bleb-forming devices are scarce: the guide identified one PreserFlo®-versus-trabeculectomy RCT and one Xen 45®-versus-trabeculectomy RCT. Its clinical recommendations rely solely on panel experience. No direct high-quality PreserFlo®-versus-Xen 45® study was available, so comparisons of their efficacy, safety, complications, and technical demands are expert opinions. Both route aqueous from the anterior chamber toward subconjunctival or sub-Tenon’s space, but differ in construction, dimensions, and insertion. Table 2 presents comparisons with trabeculectomy, including Weak recommendations to consider more concentrated MMC for PreserFlo® and less concentrated injected MMC for Xen 45®, and a Strong recommendation to use the trabeculectomy approach to topical steroids.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1 Results from the consensus meeting
document_sections.content: Surgeons with experience using both devices recorded anonymous votes on perceived efficacy, safety, and technical difficulty. Their assessments reflect expert perceptions rather than a direct comparative trial.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1.1 Efficacy
document_sections.content: For eyes without previous conjunctival surgery, surgeons rated perceived efficacy from 1 to 10, with higher values indicating greater efficacy. Mean ratings were 4.7 for Xen 45® and 7.1 for PreserFlo® microshunt. The lowest individual ratings were 2 and 6, respectively. The panel perceived PreserFlo® as more effective. Figure 1 displays these ratings.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1.2 Safety
document_sections.content: On a safety rating from 1 (very safe) to 10 (very unsafe), mean scores were 3.9 for Xen 45® and 4.0 for PreserFlo®. Opinions varied widely, but the panel generally perceived Xen 45® as safer, mainly because it was thought to cause less hypotony. Figure 2 presents these ratings.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1.3 Technical difficulty
document_sections.content: On a difficulty scale from 1 (very easy) to 10 (very difficult), mean scores were 5.1 for PreserFlo® and 5.7 for Xen 45®; responses for Xen 45® were more dispersed. The panel thought PreserFlo® had a shorter learning curve for surgeons experienced in filtration surgery, but members’ trabeculectomy experience may have influenced that judgment. Compared with trabeculectomy, Xen 45® was considered easier by 90% of participants, harder by 5%, and equally difficult by 5%. Figure 3 shows the difficulty ratings.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1.4 Surgical procedure and postoperative treatment
document_sections.content: The panel strongly recommended intraoperative mitomycin C for both bleb-forming devices because subconjunctival microshunts have a high failure risk without MMC. It weakly recommended considering a higher MMC dose with PreserFlo® than with trabeculectomy and a lower injected MMC concentration with Xen 45®. It strongly recommended following trabeculectomy strategies for antifibrotic agents and postoperative steroids.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5.1.5 Complications
document_sections.content: Experts perceived Xen 45® as safer than PreserFlo®, chiefly because of a possibly lower hypotony risk, while judging their technical demands similar. Serious, potentially sight-threatening complications of any bleb-forming operation include hypotony, bleb-associated infection, and implant exposure; the text labels awareness of these risks a strong recommendation. It also strongly recommends caution because long-term device safety remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation
document_sections.content: Bleb-forming devices produce substantial IOP reduction but are perceived as less effective than trabeculectomy. Postoperative bleb care is necessary, and revision is not unusual. Table 3 sets out Strong recommendations on primary MMC use, counseling about bleb manipulations, avoiding repeated needling or revision, considering open revision, using antifibrotics during needling or revision, and considering trabeculectomy after unsuccessful initial rescue.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.6 Phacoemulsification
document_sections.content: Coexisting cataract and glaucoma call for individualized surgery; the panel had insufficient agreement for a general approach or a strong recommendation. Decisions about combined versus staged procedures should consider disease severity and preoperative IOP. MIGS generally offers moderate IOP reduction and fewer medications in mild disease, whereas more severe glaucoma is more likely to reach a lower IOP through a bleb-forming approach, including conventional surgery. Where clinically permissible, initial phacoemulsification followed by sequential surgery should be considered. For high preoperative IOP or advanced disease, the panel preferred stand-alone bleb-forming surgery or its combination with phacoemulsification over MIGS. During combined surgery, phacoemulsification should precede device insertion.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Clinical recommendations
document_sections.content: Because evidence on MIGS and bleb-forming devices is not strong, many EGS recommendations reflect expert consensus. The panel considered ab-interno trabecular bypass appropriate for non-progressing disease with an estimated target IOP in the “mid-to-high teens” range, primarily to reduce topical medication burden. It judged safety favorable and combination with planned cataract extraction the most appropriate setting. Stand-alone use may suit special situations in which prolonged drops are unsuitable, including ocular surface disease, poor adherence, or comorbidities. Surgeons implanting Xen 45® or PreserFlo® should have experience with conventional filtration, wound-healing modulation, antimetabolites, bleb assessment, needling, and revision (strong recommendation). Careful postoperative bleb monitoring is mandatory. Although medium-term results indicate relative efficacy, these devices are not currently recommended when the target IOP must be very low; conventional filtration surgery is considered more appropriate.

document_sections.heading: Choosing wisely
document_sections.content: The consensus checklist contrasts actions to take with practices to avoid. It advises assessing angle openness, tailoring surgery to patient needs and preferences, using antifibrotics carefully, auditing results, and considering cost-effectiveness. It cautions against implant placement in a shallow anterior chamber, MIGS for a low target IOP, angle surgery without intraoperative gonioscopy experience, bleb-forming device surgery without bleb-management training and experience, and, as a general rule, more than one MIGS or bleb-forming device procedure directed at the same outflow pathway.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Key questions
document_sections.content: An initial survey approached fifty experienced European surgeons, asking each for the 10 most relevant clinical questions. Thirty surgeons from 18 countries returned 248 answers; the team prioritized 12 questions, some with subdivisions. Experts developed recommendations in three meetings between 2020 and 2022 using GRADE evidence levels high, moderate, low, and very low and recommendation strengths strong or weak. Several questions exposed gaps in evidence. Table 4 contains the question-specific conclusions and recommendations: Mitomycin C for all bleb-forming operations using trabeculectomy criteria (Level of Evidence: Low; Strength of recommendation: High); postoperative steroids and antibiotics after bleb-forming surgery on a trabeculectomy-like regimen (Low; High), with neither evidence nor consensus for a particular MIGS regimen; preference for surgical bleb revision over needling, especially for Preserflo, because of perceived durability (Low; Moderate), without agreement on timing, technique, or attempt count; and antifibrotics with needling or revision (Low; High), without agreement on 5-FU versus MMC or dose. The table concludes that MIGS appear safer than bleb-forming devices (Level of Evidence: High), while both carry risks and a MIGS implant was withdrawn; that trabeculectomy remains most effective for lowering IOP (High), with expert opinion favoring NPGS over MIGS and suggesting that some bleb-forming devices may approach certain NPGS IOP results; and that bleb-forming devices lower IOP more than MIGS (Low), based on indirect evidence rather than direct comparisons. Evidence is sparse for visual-field or structural differences. The table recommends against a further MIGS or bleb-forming device procedure using the same outflow route after failure (Low; High), without consensus on the next operation after failed bleb-forming surgery. It finds evidence insufficient to establish comparative cost-effectiveness against conventional surgery (Low). It concludes that failed MIGS is unlikely to impair subsequent conventional surgery, whereas prior bleb-forming surgery may do so (Low; Moderate). Later phacoemulsification may impair bleb-forming device function; if disease severity allows, phacoemulsification should be considered first in a sequential approach (Low), a judgment partly extrapolated from trabeculectomy because direct data are lacking. Evidence does not answer whether QoL differs between subconjunctival devices, MIGS, and trabeculectomy. Table 5 identifies non-Cochrane reviews considered methodologically acceptable.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Cost-effectiveness of innovative surgery
document_sections.content: Economic assessment helps compare clinical value and resource use; an intervention cannot be cost-effective if it costs more while being less clinically effective. A cited review assessed clinical studies published from 2005–2016 alongside several forms of economic evidence and found that limited MIGS effectiveness data left its cost-effectiveness unclear. Its authors called for larger RCTs and real-world observational studies. CADTH 2019 likewise found insufficient evidence for specific recommendations on optimal clinical use or funding, emphasizing long-term, patient-relevant and stratified outcomes, harms, and costs. Harms have often been inadequately reported in intervention trials. Reviews used for the 2020 EGS Guidelines identified 49 reliable reviews but also substantial uncertainty and sometimes small, clinically unimportant differences. They reported high-certainty evidence for IOP reduction preventing glaucoma or progression, prostaglandin analogues as the most effective IOP-lowering medication, laser trabeculoplasty as effective as first-line medication for IOP control, and trabeculectomy lowering IOP more than medication; MIGS effectiveness evidence was weak. Long-term MIGS effectiveness and sufficiently robust trial-based cost and quality-of-life indicators remain unavailable. In one small cited sample, QoL at 6 months did not differ significantly between trabeculectomy and MIGS, while trabeculectomy achieved significantly lower IOP and fewer medications. A US Medicare simulation favored trabeculectomy over Preserflo® microshunt; the guide cautions that such models rely on limited, short-follow-up MIGS effectiveness evidence. Evidence that MIGS both costs less and improves health outcomes relative to conventional surgery is missing.

document_sections.heading: 4. Recommendations for surgical innovation in glaucoma
document_sections.content: Surgical innovation includes new techniques, modified approaches, and instruments. Its development and evaluation should advance together. The IDEAL collaboration, begun in 2009, offers phases from initial idea through long-term assessment to improve safety, transparency, and evaluation. Many newer glaucoma operations have gained use without adequate evidence or long follow-up demonstrating superiority to established methods. Evaluation must account for surgeon and team skills, infrastructure, patient characteristics, and postoperative care. Outcome selection, assessor masking, learning curves, and long-term observation complicate RCTs; IDEAL provides a structured route through these challenges.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 IDEAL phases
document_sections.content: Table 6 describes IDEAL. Phase 1 generally reports first human use in a case report or short series. It calls for transparent patient selection and consent, operator and setting details, a clear technique description, safety monitoring, perioperative care, standardized validated outcomes, and adverse-event documentation for every patient; results inform whether and how to proceed safely. Phase 2a reports a refined technique through sequential, complete case-series results, including eligibility, procedural changes, outcomes, complications, and learning curves; it assesses stability and readiness for a prospective multicentre phase 2b study. Surgeon, institution, and ethics committee should agree on responsibility for risk reduction. Phase 2b explores the operation in prospective collaborative cohorts, documents adherence and learning, specifies outcomes and analyses, and assesses feasibility of an RCT or pilot study. Agreement should cover the standard technique and acceptable variants, quality standards, target population, indications, outcomes and primary-outcome power calculation, comparator, and willingness to randomize. Phase 3 compares the new method with established care; RCTs are preferred, while ethical or practical barriers may require other comparative designs. Phase 4 evaluates rare harms, outcome variation, and long-term results, ideally through prospective registries or databases using a limited set of key outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Training
document_sections.content: New operations require skill acquisition through approaches that may include observation, recordings, supervised procedures, formal courses, or simulation. An expert mentor should oversee enough operations to establish competence, with training arranged to protect safety and effectiveness. Structured programs or manufacturer accreditation may help. Patients can face greater complication risk while a surgeon is learning.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Safety and consent
document_sections.content: Consent discussions must be individualized and cover material risks, alternatives, and the fact that a procedure is novel, particularly when benefits and harms remain uncertain. A cited investigation found that Eighty percent of patients would refuse surgery if they did not know whether it was the surgeon’s first experience. Available precise outcome data should be shared. Surgeons are responsible for checking that patients understand the information sufficiently to weigh potential benefits and harms.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Clinical governance
document_sections.content: Trials of operations substantially different from usual care require rigorous governance. The guide recommends an institutional surgical innovation committee to oversee evaluation, potentially at local, regional, or national level, with a standardized approach and specialist input. Its oversight should balance caution against possible improvements in patient outcomes. All human trials should be registered in publicly accessible international databases. Prospective protocol registration improves transparency and ethical accountability, reduces duplicated trials and outcome switching, and supports analysis according to the original plan.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Summary
document_sections.content: IDEAL provides a framework for safer and more transparent introduction and evaluation of surgical advances, although it has not been widely discussed in ophthalmic research. Patients with eye conditions and ophthalmic surgeons did not participate in the cited recent COS development for novel surgery and equipment. A cited review of ophthalmic surgical RCTs found frequent omissions involving surgeon expertise, learning curves, quality assurance, reproducibility, conflicts-of-interest disclosure, and registration. The guide calls for stronger adherence to IDEAL standards by surgeons, investigators, research organizations, and journal editors.

document_sections.heading: 5. Overview of study designs
document_sections.content: The guide advocates progressing from innovation through evaluation under suitable governance using IDEAL. Phase 1 documents the new technique and its early safety and outcomes; Phase 2a examines stability; Phase 2b assesses prospective feasibility; Phase 3 compares conventional and innovative treatments in high-quality RCTs; and Phase 4 monitors uncommon harms and long-term outcomes through broad prospective records, databases, or registries.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Randomized controlled trials in glaucoma
document_sections.content: RCTs limit bias and confounding, and a new technology claiming greater efficacy than an established option should undergo randomized testing. Trials entail expense, delay, and possible limits to generalizability when participants differ from usual-care populations. Most treated glaucoma progresses slowly. Trials comparing effective treatments may therefore need substantially more participants or longer follow-up than trials against placebo. Attrition is particularly relevant in older cohorts: in a 10-year trial, the text notes that 50% loss to follow-up and a 25% death rate would not be surprising. Surgical morbidity must be balanced against long-term benefit. QoL can be difficult to use as a primary outcome because vision-related changes may become detectable only in very advanced disease, whereas many trials enroll early glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1 Randomised controlled trials evaluating surgical innovations
document_sections.content:
Surgical RCT outcomes depend on surgeon skill and learning, team performance, and perioperative care. For glaucoma innovation trials, the guide considers IOP at 1-2 years an efficient and valid primary outcome without necessarily assessing long-term progression within the RCT; longer-term safety and effectiveness can be captured through EPRs. Trial recruitment discussions must explain risks, benefits, and uncertainty. Local outcomes with existing operations, surgeon preferences, and differences between study centers can affect recruitment and generalizability. Patients and clinicians may resist randomization, especially when one intervention is perceived as more invasive. Patient-preference or expertise-based designs may address particular barriers. RCTs generally lack power to quantify rare serious surgical harms; large real-world datasets, registries, and broad EPR use can help measure their incidence, severity, timing, and variation between surgeons.

Results from centres with unusually strong outcomes may not generalise to other settings; conversely, control outcomes at centres introducing a new procedure may fall short of established standards. Patients and clinicians may resist randomisation, especially when treatment arms differ in perceived invasiveness. Patient preference trials, such as REFLUX, have been proposed for this difficulty; expertise-based trials, such as KAT, may address differences in surgeon skills or equipoise. Surgical adverse effects can be rare but serious, and most trials cannot reliably compare rare events. An example across ophthalmology is sight-threatening endophthalmitis after intravitreal injection, with an incidence of <1:1000 cases. Large real-world datasets and registries matter for safety assessment, but broad EPR use may best provide continuing measurement of rare complications by incidence, severity and timing. EPRs can also support real-time comparisons of complication rates among surgeons using the same technique.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2 ‘Real world data’ and the value of EPRs
document_sections.content: Retrospective surgical reports have examined individual surgeons, surgeon groups, experience levels and training approaches. EPR datasets enable much larger audits and more precise estimates of uncommon outcomes, but missing information remains a major weakness. Records may be incomplete accidentally or cases with favourable outcomes may be selected deliberately. Requiring consecutive cases can reduce selection bias: a UK multicentre trabeculectomy audit requested 50 consecutive operations per surgeon within a defined period. Retrospective audits also lack a prospectively specified hypothesis and outcomes, permitting hypotheses to be shaped after results are known; this risk is particularly relevant when investigators strongly favour a technique. Prospective registration of an RCT protocol and analysis plan, together with restraint in post hoc analyses, helps address this problem. Real-world datasets can be more generalisable and can estimate rare, severe harms. Weak premarket safety evidence and inadequate postmarket monitoring have previously allowed uncommon but devastating device complications to go unnoticed. Regression to the mean is important when an unusually high IOP prompts recruitment and IOP change is subsequently measured: repeat measurements may be lower even without an intervention. The effect is often in the 5-6 mmHg range and can exaggerate apparent MIGS efficacy in non-comparative studies. In a comparative RCT it should affect both arms equally, although efficacy may still be overestimated. Digital collection and accessible storage of glaucoma measurements, imaging and visual-function data have developed gradually; comprehensive EPR replacement of paper records became realistic only in the last 20 years. Medisoft has been used by over half of UK eye units for over 18 years and has supported shared, anonymised analyses through the Royal College of Ophthalmologists ‘National Ophthalmology Database’. A prospective audit of 180,114 UK cataract surgeries found that posterior capsular rupture (PCR) was associated with an eightfold increase in endophthalmitis risk and a 42-fold increase in postoperative retinal detachment risk. Its overall PCR rate was 1.95%, with a somewhat higher rate among trainees. Large prospectively collected Medisoft datasets have also informed UK studies of selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT). EPRs can measure rare harms more precisely than a practicable RCT of comparable size. Evidence from trials and EPR-based audits should be considered together, accounting for each design’s advantages and limitations.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2.1 Surgical registries
document_sections.content: Formal registries can track adoption of new glaucoma devices while collecting information prospectively, unlike retrospective audits. As use and reporting increase, their datasets become more capable of detecting uncommon but serious harms. Registry value depends on its management. Surgeons performing a novel procedure should be required to submit outcome data. Proposed foundations for an effective registry include oversight by a steering committee, explicit objectives, initial and continuing funding, national or international stakeholder collaboration, a dedicated management team, agreement on the dataset, established data-processing systems, anticipation of obstacles and measures to improve completeness. The chapter advocates publicly registering every developmental step of a new surgical technique, using prospective case series before trials, testing efficacy in randomised trials whenever feasible, using other prospective designs when randomisation is impracticable, and widely employing prospective databases and registries for continuing effectiveness and safety surveillance. The IDEAL Framework supplies the structured developmental approach.

document_sections.heading: 6. How to present data from glaucoma surgical trials
document_sections.content: The chapter sets out how to present endpoints from trials of glaucoma surgery.

document_sections.heading: Good Clinical Practice (GCP)
document_sections.content: Successful surgery halts or substantially slows glaucoma progression without substantially harming vision or quality of life. Visual function and quality of life are conceptually close to the desired outcomes but require large samples and prolonged observation. IOP is therefore the principal surgical-trial endpoint: evidence links its reduction to slower progression and relates the amount of reduction to preservation of function. Inconsistent reporting obstructs comparisons and interpretation; one review of 100 studies found 92 definitions of IOP-related success. The European Glaucoma Society and others proposed simpler reporting criteria, also recommended by WGA Guidelines in 2008.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Intraocular pressure
document_sections.content: The following subsections address IOP measurement, baseline and target values, definitions of success, and failure after glaucoma surgery.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1 Tonometry
document_sections.content: Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) is the reference method for surgical trials and supports comparisons between studies. Instruments need regular calibration. Ideally, each time point includes 2-3 readings, with the dial reset to a random lower value before each reading. Other commonly used instruments include air-puff tonometers, such as Ocular Response Analyser®, and the iCare® rebound tonometer. Measures such as a two-investigator technique can reduce observer bias. Central corneal thickness (CCT) can raise or lower a GAT reading, but should not alter the comparison when both trial arms undergo baseline and subsequent measurements.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2 Defining baseline IOP
document_sections.content: Baseline IOP anchors the assessment of each person’s longitudinal change, yet preoperative measurements are seldom standardised across heterogeneous patients. Studies commonly use the recruitment or immediately preoperative value, measured during treatment, after washout or without prior treatment. Washout may be unsafe in established disease, so measurements frequently reflect topical treatment, with or without systemic medication. The latest measurement is commonly chosen; the median of the last two or three readings is more robust when feasible. Peak IOP is too variable for a baseline and can distort before-and-after comparisons. Recruiting because IOP is high makes regression to the mean unavoidable when IOP change is the outcome, substantially exaggerating the apparent surgical effect; the problem may be smaller when visual-field findings determine surgery.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.3 Target IOP
document_sections.content: Surgery aims to lower postoperative IOP substantially below preoperative IOP. Although EGS Guidelines favour individual targets in routine care, a trial should define its success target in advance. An absolute upper IOP limit and a percentage reduction can both be used, and reporting more than one criterion set is recommended. Illustrative criteria are ≤21 mmHg with a 25% reduction in mild or early disease, and 18 mmHg with 30% reduction or 15 mmHg with 40% reduction in more advanced disease.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.4 Success as an outcome parameter
document_sections.content: Meeting an endpoint without added postoperative medication is generally termed “complete success”; meeting it with added medication is “qualified success”. Qualified success is difficult to compare when surgeons independently decide whether to restart medication. Using medication reduction as a primary outcome is similarly prone to bias. Several MIGS RCT reports have used postoperative discontinuation or reduction in drops, sometimes expressed as the proportion of drop-free participants. That outcome can help estimate comparative efficacy, but its suitability as a success criterion is questionable unless postoperative prescribing follows a predefined algorithm rather than clinician and patient preference.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.5 Failed IOP control, visual loss, and further surgery
document_sections.content: Failure includes IOP above a preset target, usually on two consecutive visits, severe postoperative visual loss caused by a complication, or another surgical intervention. Suturelysis, Nd:YAG laser goniopuncture, antimetabolite injections and needlings are not classified as failures, but should still be reported.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Visual acuity
document_sections.content: Because IOP-lowering surgery should preserve acuity, visual acuity is a safety endpoint. A fall in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of >2 Snellen lines, equivalent to doubling of logMAR values, is generally clinically relevant and warrants an explanation. BCVA is unsuitable as the primary endpoint because macular or retinal disease unrelated to surgery is common in older participants. Standardised preoperative and postoperative tests, such as ETDRS charts, should be used, with starting and final acuity displayed in a table or scatterplot. Very poor vision may be categorised as hand movements (HM), light perception (LP) or no light perception (NLP); for analysis these correspond to 1/800 (logMAR 2.3), 1/1600 (logMAR 2.8) and 1/3200 (logMAR >3), respectively. Loss of ≥ 3 ETDRS lines, equivalent to doubling of the visual angle, such as 10/10 to 5/10, is moderate; loss of ≥ 6 lines, equivalent to quadrupling, such as 8/10 to 2/10, is severe. Studies should report the percentages and causes of these losses to assess and compare safety.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Visual field parameters
document_sections.content: Despite subjectivity and confounding by media opacities such as cataract, VF testing is the measurable outcome most closely related to functional glaucoma impairment. At least 2 preoperative tests should establish baseline, and study designs should specify postoperative testing; an inadequate postoperative schedule is a frequent weakness. Preoperative and postoperative MD may suffice in shorter, early-innovation trials. At a 2-year evaluation horizon, VF results should be reported, with frequent testing needed to detect progression over that interval.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Structural outcomes
document_sections.content: Structural measures are generally unsuitable for early surgical-innovation evaluations because short studies detect change poorly. RNFL measurements may reach a floor in advanced disease; macular disease and concurrent cataract surgery add further difficulties or bias. Imaging may contribute to longer studies (>5 years).

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Quality of life
document_sections.content: QoL outcomes have been proposed for glaucoma trials, but vision-related questionnaire effects may appear only in very advanced disease, while many medication and device trials enrol people with early glaucoma. The guide notes previously described limitations of QoL as a trial endpoint.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 Overall data presentation
document_sections.content: Tables are recommended for baseline characteristics and outcomes covering IOP, medication, visual function and complications. Suggested graphics show IOP distribution through follow-up, surgical-success survival under possibly several criteria, preoperative versus postoperative IOP scatterplots, medication use and BCVA.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.1 Mean or median IOP values
document_sections.content: Postoperative IOP summaries should include dispersion. Mean ± standard deviation (M±SD) is common, but standard error (SEM) should not be used. Because IOP is seldom normally distributed, median and interquartile range are usually preferable. Figure 4 illustrates preoperative and 2 years of follow-up medians, boxes at the 25/75 percentiles, whiskers at the 5/95 percentiles and individual outliers.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.2 Kaplan-Meier curve
document_sections.content: A Kaplan-Meier display of time to failure should be considered mandatory. Survival is ordinarily based on prespecified target-IOP success rules. Curves should show group sizes at every follow-up point, including censored observations, and, where possible, the 95%-confidence interval. Figure 5 illustrates 1-year success under two criteria.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.3 Scatterplot
document_sections.content: An IOP scatterplot represents each eye by its baseline and postoperative values. The y=x line indicates no change; lower postoperative IOP falls beneath it. Separate symbols can identify complete and qualified success. Lines indicating relative reductions of 20, 30 and 40% and absolute thresholds of 12, 15, 18 and 21 mmHg can aid interpretation; readers can apply their own criteria. In the Figure 6 example, the joint criteria are ≤18 mmHg and ≥30% reduction: all but 3 eyes met the absolute IOP threshold, while another 15 failed the percentage criterion. Its symbols distinguish procedures A and B with and without medication.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.4 Preoperative versus postoperative medication
document_sections.content: A table of postoperative IOP-lowering drugs may accompany an IOP graph. Being drop-free is relevant to patients but may exaggerate differences between arms and is especially susceptible to bias when clinicians decide independently whether to prescribe. Assessment is difficult without standardised prescribing criteria, ideally implemented by a masked external trial centre. Studies usually compare average preoperative and final medication use. For statistical analysis of medication counts, median and box plots are preferable: with nonparametric, low-valued counts, mean ± standard deviation can yield standard-deviation limits below 0.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.5 Graphical representation of visual acuity
document_sections.content: Starting and final acuity can be tabulated or plotted. Averages should use logMAR rather than decimal acuity because the underlying visual scale is logarithmic. For analysis, HM corresponds to 1/800 (logMAR 2.3), LP to 1/1600 (logMAR 2.8) and NLP to 1/3200 (logMAR >3). Figure 7 compares preoperative and postoperative acuity at 2 yrs for two matched surgical methods, separately identifying phakic and pseudophakic eyes.

document_sections.heading: 6.7 Methods of analysis and reporting
document_sections.content: Study teams need close collaboration with a clinical trials unit (CTU), statisticians and researchers experienced in trial design, delivery and analysis. The following subsections address statistical descriptions and reporting.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.1 Descriptive statistics
document_sections.content: Continuous data should be assessed for compatibility with a normal distribution and then presented as mean or median with a suitable dispersion measure, such as SD or interquartile range. Frequencies can describe categorical and nominal data.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.2 Minimal clinically important difference (MCID)
document_sections.content: Statistical significance of between-group or before-and-after differences does not by itself establish clinical importance; inadequate sample size also creates a risk of type II error. Investigators are encouraged to specify the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for important endpoints before a study. MCID represents the smallest outcome difference patients can perceive as beneficial or harmful and can inform whether treatments are sufficiently similar or different to change care. Prespecification also supports sample-size calculation without unnecessary under- or oversampling. A single MCID may not suit every population, setting, disease stage, health status or comorbidity profile. Glaucoma research has concentrated largely on patient-reported MCIDs, without an agreed MCID for IOP or other clinical endpoints. Proposed ways to establish one include distribution-, expert-opinion- and anchor-based approaches. A UK specialist survey and an EGS expert discussion identified 2-3 mmHg as the IOP MCID for glaucoma surgery. For the proportion medication-free, most EGS experts favoured 20 to 30%, conditional on standardised rules for restarting drops. Most judged that the between-intervention MCID for global visual-field indices should be not less than 2 dB. Interpretation should account for follow-up duration, population and intervention. Where standards remain unsettled, investigators are strongly encouraged to report their chosen MCID, justification and selection method. The accompanying MCID summary shows the expert-panel IOP value as 2-3 mmHg and the medication-free value as 20-30% of study subjects.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.3 Kaplan-Meier curves
document_sections.content: Kaplan–Meier curves are highly recommended to compare time-to-event IOP outcomes between groups using <21, <18, <15 and <12 mmHg thresholds.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.4 Missing data
document_sections.content: Both per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses are highly recommended. For every endpoint, investigators must give the number analysed at each follow-up time point.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.5 Standards for reporting
document_sections.content: Every randomised clinical trial should follow Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT). Available standards for nonrandomised and observational research should also be applied to early IDEAL phase 1 and 2 evaluations, including relevant CONSORT and STROBE extensions. PROCESS may provide a reporting structure for case series; investigators are encouraged to consider SUPER for detailed surgical-technique reporting across case reports, series, observational studies and randomised trials. The chapter’s reporting summary favours prespecified trial success criteria combining an IOP ceiling and percentage reduction, regards Kaplan-Meier time-to-failure curves as necessary graphical reporting, identifies scatterplots as useful and warns that postoperative medication reduction is highly vulnerable to bias as a success measure.

document_sections.heading: 7. Complications
document_sections.content: Evidence about glaucoma-surgery harms comes from case reports, retrospective analyses, prospective cohorts and randomised trials. Prospective protocols provide the best opportunity for complete, consistent, prespecified capture. CONSORT and PRISMA offer reporting guidance. In one trabeculectomy cohort, changing success definitions altered success estimates by nearly 50%, illustrating the need for consistent criteria. Published studies also differ substantially in complication lists, definitions and reporting times, obstructing comparisons. Accurate, consistent descriptions of harms and their severity support informed treatment decisions; quality of life and continued independence are especially important to patients.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Definition of complications
document_sections.content: A glaucoma-surgery complication must be an unintended, undesirable direct consequence of an operation that would not reasonably have occurred if the procedure had gone as expected. It must also be sufficiently specific: a nonspecific label such as infections is inadequate. Harms can be common across procedures or particular to a surgical category. The chapter points to an overview for standardised general and procedure-specific reporting and to more detailed definitions developed by the EGS consensus group. Table 7 lists proposed definitions, including IOP and acuity thresholds and graded anterior-chamber and hyphema findings; the later templates list complications by procedure.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Severity grading
document_sections.content: Complications vary in their consequences for patients and potential effect on quality of life, so frequency alone is insufficient. No standardised method currently captures patient harm. Discussions usually begin at consent and become more detailed if harm occurs. A glaucoma-specialist consensus exercise graded the severity of a limited selection of complications, but broader evaluation and more patient-friendly severity measures are still needed.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Timing of harm reporting
document_sections.content: Studies often omit when a postoperative harm arose. The guide proposes, as a reasonable approach rather than a fixed universal definition, classifying an event within 3 months of surgery as early and one after 3 months as late, because healing is normally complete by then.

document_sections.heading: 7.4 Reporting complications
document_sections.content: Surgical trials should plan safety reporting before recruitment. Protocols should specify adverse events, whether they are expected or unexpected and related or unrelated to treatment, and investigator-defined counts and descriptions of serious and non-serious complications. Table 7 offers candidate definitions, while Tables 8 to 13 provide procedure-specific reporting templates and graphical approaches. Graphics can communicate a harm’s frequency, timing and severity rapidly to clinicians and potentially patients.

document_sections.heading: 8. Outcomes for clinical trials
document_sections.content: The chapter addresses inconsistent selection of trial outcomes and describes shared outcomes and descriptors for studies of glaucoma surgical innovation.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 The problem of outcome multiplicity
document_sections.content: Trials assess an intervention by comparing measured effects and harms between treatment groups. Such results inform care only if outcomes matter to patients, professionals and other decision-makers. When studies of the same topic measure different things, meaningful comparison becomes difficult. Outcome heterogeneity has been documented across medicine and ophthalmology; as many as 40% of recent Cochrane reviews across topics identified it as an obstacle to synthesis.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 What are core outcome sets?
document_sections.content: A core outcome set (COS) is a stakeholder-agreed minimum of standardised outcomes to measure and report in every trial within a defined healthcare area. Its adoption should make those outcomes consistently available, without preventing investigators from collecting additional endpoints relevant to a particular trial.

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Core outcome set development
document_sections.content: The following subsections describe whose preferences should inform a COS, how agreement is reached and why common outcomes can improve evidence synthesis.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.1 Stakeholder involvement
document_sections.content: COS development should reflect the priorities of healthcare practitioners, trialists, regulators, industry representatives, policymakers, researchers, patients, other service users and the public.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.2 Steps of core outcome set development
document_sections.content: Development usually begins with a systematic review of potential endpoints and continues with stakeholder consensus on which are most important. Agreement initially concerns what to measure; some projects also agree on measurement instruments. Formal iterative approaches such as the Delphi method are commonly used.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.3 COMET database and core outcome sets in Ophthalmology
document_sections.content: The Core Outcome Measures for Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative connects groups developing and applying COSs, shares resources and supports methodological research. Its freely accessible COMET Database lists completed and ongoing sets. Development varies by specialty. The guide reports a low number in ophthalmology, three, mentioning geographic atrophy, age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma, while also stating that none is specific for glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.4 Advantages of core outcome sets
document_sections.content: COSs let stakeholders influence which endpoints trials measure and give trials a common minimum suitable for systematic review and meta-analysis. Shared evidence can then support regulatory decisions, healthcare guidance and clinical choices. Trial investigators, funders, registries, regulators, review groups, guideline developers and journal editors increasingly endorse their use.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.5 Summary
document_sections.content: Shared outcome sets may reduce between-trial heterogeneity. The guide calls for greater involvement and leadership from COS researchers and relevant stakeholders, with the intended downstream benefits of more useful trials, stronger reviews, better-informed guidance and improved health decisions.

document_sections.heading: 8.4 Outcomes and descriptors for glaucoma studies evaluating surgical innovations
document_sections.content: No COS had been established for trials of new glaucoma operations. Variable outcome reporting limits comparisons and the usefulness of RCT findings. EGS therefore worked with experienced glaucoma surgeons on a proposed COS, descriptors and a clinical research form (CRF) for data collection. Future development needs patient and other stakeholder participation.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.1 Methology
document_sections.content: Development involved a 3-step process: identify published outcomes and descriptors from studies and reviews; ask experts to grade their relevance electronically; and seek expert consensus during two in-person meetings. The framework distinguishes exploratory or efficacy studies at IDEAL phase 2 from definitive effectiveness studies at IDEAL phase 3. Items are designated “Highly Recommended” or “Optional”. Descriptor domains cover population, surgical procedure and follow-up time; outcome domains cover clinical effectiveness, including IOP, further interventions, visual function and OCT structure, as well as QoL, PROM and safety. Analysis domains cover descriptive statistics, charts, methods and reporting. Table 14 displays the proposed items, their categories and follow-up schedules.

document_sections.heading: Table 14
document_sections.content: The table sets out which population and surgical-procedure descriptors, follow-up visits, efficacy and safety outcomes, and analysis and reporting practices are “Highly Recommend” or “Optional”. It includes notes qualifying particular early follow-up and progression assessments.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.2 Descriptors
document_sections.content: The following subsections explain the proposed descriptions of study populations, surgical techniques, antimetabolite use and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.2.1 Population
document_sections.content: Clinical studies of surgical innovation need detailed population descriptions. Recommended characteristics include demographics, general and ocular health, lens status, comorbidity, past interventions, and structural and functional glaucoma measures. Unmedicated preoperative IOP after washout, CCT and OCT-derived structural measures are optional.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.2.2 Surgical procedures
document_sections.content: Because operator skill can affect a complex operation’s outcome, surgeon experience with each studied technique is a “highly recommended” descriptor. Learning curves differ between techniques and innovation stages. In the absence of a more standardised measure, the number of procedures previously performed is the best available surrogate.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.2.3 Use of antimetabolites in bleb-forming techniques
document_sections.content: Antifibrotics can substantially change filtering-surgery outcomes, so related studies should describe their use. Details include agent type, such as MMC, 5FU or topical steroids; dose, including concentration, volume and exposure time; and application method, such as sponges or subconjunctival injection.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.2.4 Follow-up time points
document_sections.content: An early-stage, short-term efficacy study does not necessarily need prolonged follow-up to be clinically useful. Nonetheless, visit timing affects accurate and prompt assessment of efficacy and safety; testing frequency should match the endpoint, likely timing of change and time since surgery. For most outcomes the proposed minimum highly recommended visits are 1 week, 1 month and 3-6-12 months; studies extending beyond 12 months may schedule visits every 6 months. The chapter subsequently describes Day 1 as “highly recommended” only when a technique is early in development and its immediate postoperative course is poorly understood. Table 14 also identifies the 1 day * visit as optional and notes its relevance to early-stage techniques.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3 Outcomes
document_sections.content: The outcome framework addresses efficacy, safety and quality of life in studies of new glaucoma operations.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1 Efficacy
document_sections.content: Efficacy reporting encompasses IOP, ocular hypotensive medication, subsequent interventions, perimetry and structural imaging.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1.1 IOP
document_sections.content: IOP is usually the primary endpoint for novel surgical interventions and requires a clear, standard definition. Reporting its mean and both absolute (mmHg) and relative (%) changes from baseline, with a suitable dispersion measure such as standard deviation, is mandatory. Reporting patient proportions below prespecified follow-up thresholds of <21, <18, <15 and <12 mmHg further describes outcome distribution. Investigators should make every possible effort to mask IOP assessors. Where slit-lamp observation might reveal allocation, an external observer or two-observer procedure can reduce bias. Substituting tonometers other than GAT may hinder between-study comparisons.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1.2 Ocular hypotensive medications
document_sections.content: Without prospectively standardised prescribing criteria, follow-up medication can seriously bias estimates of efficacy and comparisons between operations. Trials must describe their rules for restarting and escalating topical or systemic hypotensive treatment, even though the rules may vary across trials. At every study time point they must report the mean/SD count of topical medications by active principle and the numbers and percentages of medicated and unmedicated patients.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1.3 Postoperative interventions
document_sections.content: Trials must count additional procedures undertaken to control IOP or manage complications. IOP-control procedures include needling, suture lysis or removal, surgical revision and further glaucoma surgery. Because a participant can require repeated treatment, reporting the number and % of patients undergoing 0, 1, 2 or more postoperative interventions is also highly recommended.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1.4 Perimetry
document_sections.content: Standard automated perimetry measures visual function relevant to both efficacy and safety. Between-treatment differences in progression matter for long-term glaucoma management, although innovation trials do not invariably need prolonged observation. If VF is assessed, reporting the mean and SD of mean deviation or mean defect at appropriate visits is highly recommended. Accurate progression-rate estimates require frequent tests or longer observation; the prose calls these assessments “highly recommended” only for studies exceeding 2 years, while Table 14 marks preoperative and postoperative RoP ** as optional and notes studies longer than 2 years. Severe field loss may be treated as a complication.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.1.5 Optical Coherence Tomography
document_sections.content: Structural measurements from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) may help in surgical trials but are classified “optional”.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.2 Safety
document_sections.content: Reporting the number and % of every complication is highly recommended, as is reporting the number and % of patients experiencing 0, 1, 2 or more postoperative complications. Harms should be classified as intraoperative or postoperative; early or late relative to 3 months after surgery; and serious and sight-threatening or nonserious. IOP readings lower than 6 mmHg should be reported because they are common after many procedures. The guide reserves the label of clinically relevant hypotony as an adverse event for symptomatic low IOP. Table 14 separately labels early complications (<1 month) and late complications (≥3 month), whereas the prose describes timing relative to 3 months.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.2.1 Endothelial corneal cells
document_sections.content: Surgery can damage endothelial corneal cells (ECCs). Reporting the mean/median absolute cell count and mean % reduction from baseline is “highly recommended”. Absolute mean/median change is optional because baseline count and follow-up percentage allow it to be calculated. Trials must additionally report the number and % of participants whose ECC loss exceeds 20, 30, and 40% of baseline.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.2.2 Visual acuity
document_sections.content: BCVA is a highly recommended endpoint, particularly for safety. The chapter refers to its earlier measurement and reporting guidance. Its safety summary also calls for the number and % of each complication, counts of patients with 0, 1, 2 or more complications, absolute ECC counts and mean percentage ECC loss.

document_sections.heading: 8.4.3.3 Quality of Life
document_sections.content: Preserving or improving QoL is an ultimate aim of care, making patient-reported outcomes useful alongside clinical endpoints. No accepted reference instrument exists for glaucoma intervention studies. Available questionnaires address disease effects, treatment, symptoms, adverse effects, activities or overall health at a single time or longitudinally. Severity and questionnaire scores are not linearly related, and some tools show ceiling effects in early disease. Vision Related (VR) QoL measures may change only in advanced glaucoma; instruments may miss small visual-field changes; and transient early postoperative harm may precede benefits that take longer to emerge. Comparisons also become harder when trial arms differ in invasiveness. Existing instruments may not detect between-intervention differences adequately. Disease-specific, vision-related and generic instruments capture different domains. The guide treats QoL assessment as welcome but optional within the COS; Table 15 describes example questionnaires, including NEI-VFQ-25, 15-D, EQ-5D and SF6D.

document_sections.heading: Epilogue
document_sections.content: The author argues that responsible innovation begins by acknowledging shortcomings in current care and defining improvement together with each patient. Treatment goals cannot be determined by an algorithm alone: clinicians should understand patients’ fears, expectations and circumstances, explain uncertainty rather than merely recite risks, and check what patients have understood. Decisions should consider disease stage, rate and expected duration of change, likely treatment effects on disease and quality of life, socioeconomic circumstances, and the surgeon’s skills and support. The author illustrates how a frail patient with slowly worsening vision might reasonably continue current management, with review in 3 months and earlier contact if change occurs; this is an illustrative scenario, not a general recommendation. A second hypothetical case concerns a 52-year-old with advanced glaucoma and a proposed, untested filtering technique. The example emphasises disclosure that the approach has not been used in human eye surgery, that its benefit and harms are uncertain, and that surgeon enthusiasm can bias the presentation of options. The patient chooses referral instead. The author argues that respecting that choice, rather than pressuring agreement with an unproven operation, is central to patient autonomy.
